item.title: JACS: Synthetic W/Cu Mimics of the Mo/Cu Active Site in Aerobic CODH: Nonclassical Isocyanide Coordination and the Role of the Bridging Sulfide
item.description:
Mahesh Kumar Choudhary, Daniel Kim, Neal P. Mankad
Aerobic carbon monoxide dehydrogenase (CODH) uses an unsupported Mo–S–Cu heterobimetallic active site to catalyze CO oxidation, but the mechanistic role of the bridging sulfide remains to be fully resolved. We report a series of W/Cu complexes designed to test whether steric shielding from a bidentate tBuxantphos ligand can suppress unwanted Cu···Sdithiolate and Cu···O═M interactions that plagued the reactivity of a previously reported NHC-ligated model system. Addition of [Cu(tBuxantphos)]+ to [(bdt)WVI(O)(OSiiPr3)(X)]− (bdt = 1,2-benzenedithiolate; X = O, S, Se) unexpectedly favors Cu coordination at the W═O rather than the W═X unit, giving X═W–O–Cu cores as the thermodynamically preferred isomers, opposite to the connectivity predicted by hard–soft acid–base theory and found in CODH itself. The resulting complexes bind isocyanides at CuI with nonclassical (blue-shifted) C≡N stretching frequencies. In contrast, no reactivity is observed toward CO gas, consistent with DFT predictions that CO coordination is endergonic. However, the calculations reveal that the CO adduct of the hypothetical O═W–S–Cu–CO isomer is more stabilized than its S═W–O–Cu–CO counterpart, an effect traced by molecular orbital analysis to delocalization of electron density from the redox-active dithiolate through the bridging sulfide into the Cu–CO π-backbonding manifold. These results provide an electronic rather than purely structural rationale for why the CODH active site retains a bridging sulfide despite an apparent thermodynamic preference for a bridging oxo in the synthetic analogues investigated here.

item.title: ACS Nano: Effect of Chiral-Induced Spin Selectivity in Half-Metallic La0.67Sr0.33MnO3 Thin Films
item.description:
Michal Bennár, Marianna Španková, Štefan Chromik, Marcel Talacko, Iuliia Vetrova, Andrej Dvurečenskij, Alexander Cigáň, Martin Škrátek, et al.
Magnetism induced by the proximity effects of chiral molecules is a physical phenomenon that can be demonstrated with molecular layers as thin as 1 nm deposited on thin films of conventional ferromagnets. Although the chiral-induced spin selectivity effect has been widely explored in the context of spintronic applications involving charge transport through chiral molecules, due to its capacity to generate high spin polarizations at room temperature, the accompanying process of induced magnetization without applied current likewise presents opportunities for exploitation. In this work, we demonstrate that, unlike conventional ferromagnets, where the induced magnetization aligns with the chiral axis of the polymer, the CISS effect in half-metallic ferromagnets (La0.67Sr0.33MnO3) favors a quasi-perpendicular magnetization configuration. This preference for quasi-perpendicular magnetization is caused by the formation of a thermally driven steady state, which, due to different transport probabilities into the molecule, results in a modification of the domain-wall energy landscape. These results provide insight into the chiral-induced spin selectivity effect without net currents and also clarify mechanism for controlling magnetization within half-metallic thin films for spintronic devices.

item.title: JACS: Intricate Proteoform Heterogeneity in the Tailpiece of IgA within and across Its Circulatory and Secretory Configurations
item.description:
Weiwei Wang, Amber D. Rolland, Gestur Vidarsson, Johannes B. van Goudoever, Karli R. Reiding, Albert Bondt, Albert J. R. Heck
Human immunoglobulin A (IgA) naturally occurs in multiple molecular forms─monomers, dimers, and even higher-order polymers─that are differentially distributed across serum, breast milk, and mucosal surfaces. The C-terminal tailpiece of IgA is essential to its polymerization mediated by the joining chain (J-chain) and thus also an important determinant of its extensive structural heterogeneity, yet its features remain somewhat poorly defined. Here, we used HILIC-LC-MS/MS-based glycopeptide analysis to characterize the N-glycan structures, disulfide linkages, and C-terminal amino acid sequence variants within the IgA tailpiece across the different molecular configurations of endogenous IgA. We find extensive correlation between these post-translational modifications; i.e., variations in tailpiece Asn459 N-glycosylation, redox status and disulfide connectivity of Cys471, and the presence or absence of C-terminal Tyr472 are intrinsically interconnected. When Cys471 was disulfide-bound to the J-chain, Asn459 glycans showed broader structural heterogeneity and retained more high-mannose structures, whereas free Cys471 tailpieces mainly carried mature, sialylated complex-type glycans. Serum IgA and milk SIgA displayed distinct tailpiece signatures, including differences in N-glycan maturation and processing of the ultimate C-terminal Tyr472 residue. Together, these findings define biofluid-specific molecular forms of IgA and highlight the remarkable structural diversity of the human IgA tailpiece. Overall, our results advance the understanding of the IgA structure and could offer a much-needed molecular basis to assist future bioengineering of IgA-based therapeutics.

item.title: JACS: A Microporous Zr-Tetraphosphonate MOF with Permanent Porosity, Robustness, and Thermochemical Heat Storage Capability
item.description:
Pablo Salcedo-Abraira, Catalina Biglione, Sérgio M. F. Vilela, Artem A. Babaryk, Antonio Rodríguez-Diéguez, Philippe Trens, Fabrice Salles, Jerzy Zajac, et al.
Combining high-valent metal cations with phosphonate linkers represents a promising strategy to address the limited stability of MOFs, yet permanently porous phosphonate MOFs (P-MOFs) remain rare due to the strong coordination propensity of phosphonate groups. Herein, we report IEF-10, a new microporous zirconium tetraphosphonate framework constructed from ZrO5F octahedral secondary building units and a pyrene tetraphosphonate linker. The material combines three features that are seldom achieved simultaneously in P-MOFs: permanent accessible microporosity (equivalent BET surface area ∼430 m2·g–1), accessible phosphonic acid functionalities (-PO3H), and exceptional thermal (up to 450 °C), mechanical (>3 tons), and chemical stability (pH 1–12, organic solvents). The structure exhibits reversible water adsorption with moderate uptake and experimentally determined capacities of heat storage of ∼400–500 J·g–1, reflecting a favorable balance between host–guest interactions and regeneration requirements. As a proof of concept, IEF-10 was evaluated for thermochemical heat storage under dynamic moist-gas flow conditions. Calorimetric measurements revealed fast heat-release kinetics (3–4 h), and excellent cyclability in terms of heat release (at least 10 cycles, total test duration of 5 weeks). The hydrophobic surface character is an advantage for long-term storage uses as the adsorbent can remain in a dry state between the charging and discharging stages even at low relative humidity levels in the reactor. These results demonstrate how the combination of permanent porosity, accessible phosphonic acid groups, and exceptional framework robustness can enable functional adsorption-driven energy storage while providing new opportunities for the development of porous zirconium P-MOFs.

item.title: JACS: Fluorine-Mediated Molten-Salt Crystallization Regulates Phase Evolution and Structural Stability in Sodium Layered Oxides
item.description:
Chenguang Shi, Junyi Yao, Xiaowen Zhan, Jeongok Choe, Xixian Yang, He Zhou, Amir Ashraf Elnashar, Rupayan Ghosh, et al.
Ni- and Co-free P2-type Fe–Mn layered oxides with high Na concentrations are promising cathodes for sodium-ion batteries, but their practical use is limited by phase instability during Na-excess synthesis and structural degradation during cycling and storage. Although large single-crystal-like architectures could improve stability, controlled phase-selective crystallization in these cathode systems remains challenging. Here, we show that fluorine-assisted molten-salt synthesis enables controlled formation of large-particle Fe–Mn–Ti P2 cathodes with enhanced phase selectivity and structural coherence. Compared with Na-excess processing alone, NaF-assisted flux growth expands the P2 phase stability window and promotes large particles with uniform morphologies while preserving local layered ordering. Multiscale characterization further reveals more-reversible structural evolution and more homogeneous Mn redox behavior in the NaF-assisted material, together with a gradient-like fluorine distribution involving surface-enriched NaF-like species and lower level interior fluorine environments. These coupled structural, morphological, and chemical features collectively mitigate crack formation and deliver good cycling stability. In summary, NaF-assisted molten-salt synthesis shows promise in addressing key limitations of Ni- and Co-free P2-type Fe–Mn layered cathodes.

item.title: JACS: G-Quadruplex-Interacting Photooxidative Platinum(IV) Prodrug for Inhibiting Oncogene Transcription and Amplifying Antitumor Immunity
item.description:
Dengshuai Wei, Yijia Chen, Jiaqian Xu, Guangyu Zhu
Conventional platinum (Pt)-based chemotherapeutics elicit cancer cell death primarily through DNA binding, but this approach is inherently limited by poor site specificity and a lack of spatiotemporal control, which compromises therapeutic precision and safety. To overcome these limitations, we report DNATplatin, an in situ activatable and photooxidative Pt(IV) prodrug designed to combine precise recognition of DNA secondary structures with targeted genetic intervention through DNA photooxidation. By incorporating a bis-N-methylpyridinium moiety to selectively recognize DNA, DNATplatin shows a 10-fold increase in the levels in genomic DNA relative to oxaliplatin and a 2.5-fold emission turn-on selectivity for G-quadruplexes (G4s) over typical duplex DNA. Following precise nuclear localization, photoactivated DNATplatin acts as a potent photooxidant that oxidizes G4, dismantles G4 scaffolds, and abrogates circular dichroism signatures. These orchestrated lesions generate localized oxidative stress and selectively silence major G4-driven oncogenes, thereby effectively circumventing traditional Pt resistance by bypassing canonical adduct-dependent pathways. In a murine triple-negative breast tumor model, DNATplatin produces profound tumor suppression and elicits a robust systemic immune response, characterized by CD4+/CD8+ T-cell activation and depletion of Foxp3+ regulatory T cells. Collectively, this work establishes a controllable “target-and-destroy” strategy and underscores the potential of Pt(IV) photooxidants for topology-selective genetic intervention.

item.title: Nano Letters: Unidirectional Magnetoresistance Driven by Nonequilibrium Antiferromagnetic Magnons
item.description:
Xue He, Hans Gløckner Giil, Caiqiong Xu, Jicheng Wang, Arne Brataas, Jinbo Yang, Yanglong Hou, Zhaochu Luo, et al.
Magnetoresistive effects are typically symmetric under magnetization reversal. However, nonlinear spin transport can give rise to unidirectional magnetoresistance in systems with strong spin–orbit interaction and broken inversion symmetry. Here, we report a large magnonic unidirectional spin Hall magnetoresistance (USMR) in a van der Waals antiferromagnet CrPS4 in contact with Pt, driven by the nonequilibrium magnon accumulation with a finite magnon chemical potential. In contrast to conventional magnonic USMR driven by magnetization fluctuations, this effect persists under strong magnetic fields and low temperatures. The magnitude of magnonic USMR in CrPS4/Pt exceeds that of YIG/Pt by more than 2 orders of magnitude and surpasses the electrical USMR in metallic Ta/Co bilayers by a factor of 2. Our results highlight magnon chemical potential gradients for nonlinear magnetoresistance in antiferromagnetic van der Waals heterostructures and open a route to magnon-based antiferromagnetic spintronic functionalities in two-terminal device geometries.

item.title: JACS: Sugar-Based 1-Dimensional Metal–Organic Chalcogenolates with Hydration-Tunable Chiroptical Emission
item.description:
Qiaoling Fan, Adriana J. Ladera, Daniel W. Paley, Daniel M. Tchoń, Amaleswari Rasamsetty, Hawi N. Nyiera, Maggie C. Willson, David W. Mittan-Moreau, et al.
Chiral topology in semiconductors introduces a structural degree of freedom for tuning the chiroptical, excitonic, and spintronic behavior. In metal–organic chalcogenolates (MOChas) semiconductors, how ligand stereochemistry and supramolecular organization influence chiral topology, and thus optical and excitonic responses, remains poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate intrinsic circularly polarized luminescence (CPL) in sugar-based 1-dimensional MOChas, with structures solved via small-molecule serial femtosecond crystallography. These materials exhibit blue and green CPLs, arising from the chiral inorganic core. Despite the close chemical similarity between the glucose- and galactose-derived ligands, we observed dramatic differences in their inorganic structure. Silver glucosethiolate shows reversible hydration-driven photoluminescence switching with a hydration-linked emission energy. Labile water molecules in the glucose-based system correlate with a blueshift in excitonic emission. Our results suggest a new direction in the search for chirophotonic hybrid semiconductors, exploiting intrinsically chiral topologies and excitonic optical frequencies, which are sensitively modulated by ligand identity and supramolecular interactions.

item.title: ACS Nano: High-Throughput In-Operando Terahertz Time-Domain Spectroscopy of Chemical Vapor Deposited Graphene for pH Sensing
item.description:
Oliver J. Burton, Sebastian Engelbrecht, Thomas Goepfert, Ibtisam Hammad Abbasi, Linyuan Xin, Bernd M. Fischer, Hannah Joyce, Stephan Hofmann, et al.
Reliable pH sensing in liquid environments underpins applications in energy storage, biosensing, and process monitoring, yet conventional graphene-based electrical devices introduce ohmic contacts, encapsulation layers, and electrochemical artifacts that can obscure intrinsic behavior. These approaches also fail to capture the strong spatial variability of commercial CVD graphene. Here, we present a fully contactless methodology for quantifying pH-dependent conductivity of large-area CVD graphene using through-substrate reflection terahertz time-domain spectroscopy (THz-TDS). A customized liquid cell with a THz transparent window preserves unrestricted access to the graphene–electrolyte interface while enabling centimeter-scale conductivity mapping and in-operando single-point monitoring during sequential pH modulation. By integrating spatially registered Raman mapping with automated quality-metric filtering, we extract statistically robust trends across thousands of pixels rather than isolated device regions. We show that pristine monolayer graphene exhibits the highest baseline conductivity and strongest pH sensitivity, whereas O2-plasma-introduced defects systematically suppress both. This scalable, remote, and inert probing approach establishes THz-TDS as a powerful platform for high-throughput characterization and robust liquid-phase sensing in thin films and 2D systems.

item.title: ACS Nano: Electric-Field Tunable Spin Texture in Dual-Gated HfS2/Graphene van der Waals Heterostructures
item.description:
Haozhe Yang, Zhendong Chi, Eoin Dolan, Josep Ingla-Aynés, Beatriz Martín-García, Witold Skowroński, Marco Gobbi, Andrey Chuvilin, et al.
Spin–charge interconversion provides the essential link between spin information and electrical signals in spintronic devices. In spin–orbit coupled systems, spin–charge interconversion can contain multiple components associated with different spin-polarization directions, reflecting the underlying spin texture. Tuning this spin texture, therefore, provides a way to control not only the magnitude of spin–charge interconversion but also the balance among its different components. Graphene-based van der Waals heterostructures provide an attractive platform for this purpose because interfacial spin–orbit coupling can host multiple spin–charge interconversion channels that couple to different spin-polarization directions. Here, we demonstrate electric-field control of spin texture in a dual-gated HfS2/graphene van der Waals heterostructure, where independent control of carrier density and vertical electric field allows us to disentangle electrostatic doping from electric field-induced spin–orbit effects. Nonlocal spin precession measurements show that, near zero vertical electric field, spin–charge interconversion is dominated by a spin Hall component with out-of-plane spins. Increasing the vertical electric field enhances additional in-plane spin components with Rashba–Edelstein-like character, including contributions both parallel and perpendicular to the charge current. These results provide experimental evidence that a vertical electric field can reconfigure the effective spin texture and control the corresponding spin–charge interconversion components, demonstrating electrical tunability of spin–orbit functionalities.

item.title: Nano Letters: Role of Stereochemistry on Electron Transport in Peptides
item.description:
Rajarshi Samajdar, Hemani Chhabra, Moeen Meigooni, Seungjoo Yi, Xiaolin Liu, Jason L. Wu, Emad Tajkhorshid, Charles M. Schroeder
Stereochemistry underlies structure–function relationships across biology and materials science. Here, we investigate electron transport in oligopeptide stereoisomers using single-molecule experiments and computational modeling. Our results show that stereochemical modifications in tyrosine-based peptides lead to significant variations in molecular conductance and transport distance along the peptide backbone, associated with changes in aromatic side-chain interactions and electronic coupling. In alanine-based peptides, stereochemical modifications alter molecular conductance through secondary-structure interactions associated with β-turn conformations. Molecular dynamics simulations and quantum mechanical calculations reveal the molecular origins of these stereochemistry-dependent structural and electronic properties. Overall, this work shows that stereochemical modification of nonterminal amino acids provides a means to control electron transport through distinct mechanisms involving aromatic side-chain interactions and secondary structure. These results establish stereochemistry as a molecular design parameter for controlling electron transport in peptide-based electronic materials.

item.title: ACS Nano: Enhanced Magneto-Optical Kerr Effect in Nano-Magnetic Metamaterials with Near-Perfect Coherent Absorption
item.description:
Xiaofei Xiao, Tingjun Zheng, Alex Vanstone, Daniel S. Bromley, Holly Holder, Kilian D. Stenning, Jack C. Gartside, Will R. Branford, et al.
The ability to control magnetic systems without external magnetic fields has attracted attention recently, with all-optical magnetic switching showing increasing promise. Gaining fine control over light-matter interactions in magnetic nanostructures is essential for advancing opto-magnetic technologies but remains challenging because strong optical coupling must be achieved within ultrathin magnetic structures at the target wavelength. Here, we show that coherent optical interference can increase this interaction in patterned magnetic metasurfaces. Arrays of permalloy nanomagnets are placed on a thin dielectric spacer above a reflective back-plane, forming a magnetic metasurface whose reflected wavefront is defined by the nanomagnet geometry, fill factor, and spacer thickness. Destructive interference between the metasurface and back-plane reflections yields near-perfect absorption, exceeding 95% for circular nanomagnet arrays in both simulation and experiment. The absorbed power is dissipated almost entirely within the nanomagnets, with only a few percent lost in the metallic back-plane. Enhanced absorption is also accompanied by a stronger magneto-optical Kerr effect, driven by both increased light–nanomagnet interaction and reduced reflected background. These results provide a general approach for achieving high optical absorption and strong magneto-optical response in nanoscale magnetic systems, supporting advances in optically addressable spintronics, magnetic sensing, and all-optical magnetic control.

item.title: ACS Nano: Noise-Suppressed High-Performance WSe2 Phototransistors Enabled by Optically Programmed Remote Contact Doping
item.description:
Sunggyu Ryoo, Seongmin Ko, Juntae Jang, Donguk Kim, Jaehyoung Park, Youngmin Song, Yeeun Kim, Jaeyong Woo, et al.
Improving the sensitivity of two-dimensional semiconductor phototransistors requires increasing photocurrent while minimizing noise. However, conventional doping approaches often place charged dopants in or near atomically thin channels, introducing charge scattering, trap states, and noise that limit the signal-to-noise ratio. Here, we address this signal-noise trade-off in WSe2 phototransistors by using photoinduced charge trapping in patterned hBN to implement contact-selective remote doping. Under illumination with a negative gate voltage, trapped holes in hBN electrostatically n-dope WSe2 while remaining spatially separated from the transport channel. Patterned hBN confines the doping to selected regions, allowing the WSe2 near the metal electrodes to be remotely doped while leaving the channel undoped. This remote contact doping simultaneously suppressed the device noise by approximately 100–fold, reduced the effective density of electrically active traps by approximately 100–fold, and lowered the activation energy by 30–80 meV, indicating improved contact quality and more efficient carrier injection. As a result, the contact-doped phototransistors simultaneously exhibit enhanced responsivity of 99.7 A/W and a specific detectivity of 2.26 × 1011 Jones. These results establish optically programmed remote contact doping as a phototransistor-compatible contact-engineering approach to overcome the signal–noise trade-off in 2D phototransistors.

item.title: JACS: Core–Shell Structures Govern Through-Space Interactions in Triblock Copolymers toward Deep-Red Clusteroluminescence
item.description:
Zuping Xiong, Lidong Du, Xiong Liu, Changhuo Xu, Junlin Chen, Hanchen Shen, Longchen Zhu, Yingying Zhang, et al.
Green fluorescent protein (GFP) and its derivatives have transformed biological imaging, yet fluorophores that simultaneously combine biocompatibility, structural programmability, and intrinsic long-wavelength luminescence remain scarce. Here, we develop a controllable one-pot polymerization strategy to construct nonconjugated triblock copolymers that can self-assemble into core–shell clusters. By modulating the hydrophilic–hydrophobic balance of copolymer chains, the core-to-shell ratio, chain packing, and electronic through-space interactions within the clusters can be precisely regulated, enabling tunable clusteroluminescence (CL) that extends to the deep-red and near-infrared emission region. Ultrafast spectroscopy further uncovers the excited-state dynamics of these core–shell clusters and reveals how the coupled evolution of electronic states and structures governs CL generation. Moreover, the core–shell clusters enable in vivo angiography under two-photon excitation, highlighting their potential as biocompatible nanofluorophores. These findings establish core–shell engineering as a general design principle for efficient clusteroluminogens, deepen the mechanistic understanding of CL, and pave the way for next-generation nanofluorescence technologies.

item.title: Nano Letters: Boosting NIR-II Luminescence via Ca2+-Formed Band Structure Modulation in Lanthanide-Doped Nanoparticles for Deep-Tissue Bioimaging
item.description:
Zhiming Deng, Min Wei, Jiahao Chen, Aqiang Liu, Hanzhang Wang, Dandan Zheng, Zizhong Zhu, JingJin Chen, et al.
Lanthanide-doped nanoparticles with near-infrared-II (NIR-II, 1000–1700 nm) emission hold great promise for deep-tissue bioimaging, yet their luminescence efficiency is often limited by conventional sensitization pathways. Herein, we go beyond this conventional paradigm by introducing a Ca2+-formed band structure modulation in the host lattice to dramatically boost the NIR-II emission of lanthanide-doped nanoparticles. Rational doping of Ca2+ ions restructures the energy levels, enabling the probe to efficiently capture excitation energy and channel it toward NIR-II-emitting lanthanide activators. This Ca2+-induced band structure modulation mechanism not only enhances the absorption cross section but also accelerates energy transfer to the NIR-II-emitting states. As a result, the designed nanoprobes exhibit excellent photostability and a high quantum yield. In vivo bioimaging demonstrates that the resulting nanoprobes enable deep-tissue visualization with an improved signal-to-background ratio. This work establishes a sensitization strategy that goes beyond conventional approaches, positioning lanthanide-based NIR-II probes as promising candidates for advanced biological imaging.

item.title: ACS Nano: Gas Separation through Graphene Nanopores Enabled by Thermally Robust Porous Organic Polymer Reinforcement
item.description:
Ranadip Goswami, Shuqing Song, Yueqing Shen, Ceren Kocaman, Jian Hao, Himan Dev Singh, Wendy L. Queen, Kumar Varoon Agrawal
Porous single-layer graphene (PG) offers an ideal platform for molecular-sieving membranes due to its atomically thin inorganic lattice and its ability to incorporate molecularly selective pores. However, the use of PG for high-temperature gas separation remains limited by the lack of a mechanically reinforcing film (MRF) that enables crack-free transfer onto porous supports and stable operation under pressurization. Here, we introduce a fluorinated porous organic polymer (FPOP) that provides the mechanical and thermal robustness needed to operate PG membranes at high temperature. The FPOP layer is deposited directly on PG from a molecular precursor solution. Upon drying and thermal annealing, it develops into a continuous cross-linked film that conforms to PG, maintains strong adhesion, and helps to avoid crack formation during the transfer of PG to a macroporous support. The FPOP film exhibits a quasi-ordered structure, forms an interface with graphene, and remains stable under pressurized conditions up to 350 °C. FPOP-supported PG membranes exhibit selective gas transport at elevated temperature (350 °C) and maintain their performance during extended mixed-gas operation. The membranes retain selective transport after humid/oxidative exposure and ambient storage. Importantly, the porous FPOP can regulate transport through enlarged nonselective graphene defects, thereby improving the selectivity of PG membranes. Overall, we demonstrate FPOP as a thermally stable MRF platform that enables crack-free PG transfer, high-temperature operation, and regulation of nonselective transport pathways.

item.title: ACS Nano: Nano-Bioadhesives for Gastrointestinal Hemostasis and Healing: Integrating Artificial Intelligence for Precision Design and Application
item.description:
Menglu Wu, Xianglong Xing, Xiang Ling, Juncen Zhou, Malcolm Xing, Donghui Zhu
Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding and mucosal injury remain clinically challenging because most bioadhesives lose performance under acidic, enzymatic, and peristaltic conditions. Nanotechnology has advanced adhesive design by enhancing mechanical integrity, degradation control, and antimicrobial activity; however, translating these gains into consistently favorable clinical outcomes is still difficult. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a route to accelerate and derisk development. Here, we identify predictive, multiobjective materials design as the AI domain most critical for GI nanobioadhesives because adhesion, hemostasis, degradation, biosafety, and healing must be optimized simultaneously. Predictive modeling, molecular simulations, and high-throughput experimentation enable rational control of adhesion strength, degradation kinetics, and biocompatibility, while machine-learning models expedite the discovery of optimal polymeric nanoparticle formulations. Emerging strategies such as digital twins and closed-loop optimization further support patient-specific and adaptive adhesive systems. By integrating AI-guided design with nanotechnology platforms, next-generation GI bioadhesives could unify rapid hemostasis, antimicrobial protection, and regenerative functions, thereby improving reliability and clinical translation. This review outlines the synergy between AI and nanotechnology and highlights priorities for advancing GI adhesive therapies from bench to bedside.

item.title: JACS: Modifier-Driven Proton Conductivity in Hybrid Glasses above 200 °C
item.description:
Ellan K. Berdichevsky, Motoyasu Yamasaki, Takuya Kurihara, Taichi Nishiguchi, Siyuan Ye, Koki Ando, Yuta Hashiguchi, Hiromitsu Uehara, et al.
Compositional tuning is a cornerstone of inorganic glass science, yet analogous strategies remain underdeveloped for emerging metal–organic hybrid glasses. We introduce phosphate modification of zinc imidazolate glass as a route to hybrid glasses with tunable network connectivity and proton-conductive functionality. Melt-quenching of ZIF-zni with benzimidazolium dihydrogen phosphate (BP) affords a series of cm-scale, transparent bulk glasses across a wide compositional range. Systematic characterization reveals that modification proceeds through ligand exchange at zinc centers, increasing the average coordination number from 4 to above 5 and progressively depolymerizing the imidazolate network. Despite macroscopic homogeneity, X-ray total scattering identifies a quasi-periodic ordering at ∼11 Å, and 1H NMR spin relaxation establishes nanoscale phase segregation between ZIF-derived and BP-rich domains of 2–70 nm. This heterogeneity underpins proton transport under anhydrous conditions; conductivities of 10–5–10–3 S cm–1 at 240 °C follow Vogel–Tammann–Fulcher dynamics, confirming that segmental motion couples to ion mobility. Infiltrating the glass into a porous PTFE scaffold yields a composite membrane that achieves 8.4 × 10–5 S cm–1 at 170 °C under humidification and sustains steam electrolysis with near-unity Faradaic efficiency. These results establish network-modified hybrid glasses as a scalable and designable platform for intermediate-temperature solid electrolytes.

item.title: JACS: Crossover from Asymmetric to Symmetric Electrowetting Linked to Double-Layer Restructuring
item.description:
Hannah O. Wood, Sittipong Kaewmorakot, Jan Dočkal, Martin Lísal, Robert A. W. Dryfe, Paola Carbone
Voltage-controlled wetting at solid–liquid interfaces is central to the performance of a range of electrochemical and microfluidic technologies, yet the molecular basis of polarity-dependent electrowetting remains unresolved. Classical electrocapillarity predicts a symmetric dependence of contact angle on applied potential, but experiments and simulations frequently exhibit pronounced asymmetry. Here, combining electrowetting measurements with atomistic simulations, we show that asymmetric wetting at aqueous carbon interfaces arises from the structure of the electrical double layer. By investigating aqueous KF and LiCl electrolytes at graphitic interfaces across lower concentration and water-in-salt regimes, we identify a crossover from strongly asymmetric electrowetting at lower concentration to a symmetric response at high concentration for KF, while LiCl retains a pronounced asymmetry. This transition is accompanied by corresponding changes in the solid–liquid interfacial tension, demonstrating that polarity-dependent wetting can arise from voltage-dependent molecular restructuring of the interfacial liquid, which modifies the interfacial thermodynamics, without invoking faradaic processes. We introduce interfacial connectivity, defined by the network of intermolecular interactions within the first adsorption layer, as a molecular descriptor linking double-layer structure to macroscopic wetting behavior. These results demonstrate that electrolyte-controlled electrowetting can recover the symmetric electrocapillary limit under appropriate conditions and establish a unified framework connecting double-layer structure, interfacial free energy, and voltage-dependent wetting.

item.title: Nano Letters: From Dense to Nanostructured Thin Film Anodes: Boosting Li-Ion Accessibility in TiO2 Thin Film Electrodes
item.description:
Ravikant Adalati, Jerome Muller, Pavel Moskovkin, Abdel Ghafour El Hachimi, Stephane Lucas, Suyog Asaram Raut, Thi Thao Nguyen, Aline Roobroeck, et al.
Dense TiO2 thin-film electrodes suffer from limited electrolyte penetration and restricted Li-ion transport, making the electrode architecture a critical parameter for efficient charge storage. Herein, glancing-angle deposition (GLAD) combined with reactive magnetron sputtering is used to engineer ion-accessible TiO2 nanocolumnar architectures without compositional modification or postprocessing. Kinetic Monte Carlo simulations guided the selection of substrate tilt and azimuthal rotation conditions to control the column orientation, intercolumnar spacing, and open porosity. The predicted morphologies were subsequently validated by electron microscopy for the experimentally deposited thin films. Electrochemical measurements show that GLAD-engineered electrodes deliver up to approximately 4-fold higher areal capacitance than dense TiO2 films. ToF-SIMS depth profiling further reveals that Li species remain largely concentrated near the surface of dense films. In contrast, the GLAD-engineered nanocolumnar architecture allows for a more uniform Li distribution throughout the electrode depth. These results establish morphology-controlled ion accessibility as the primary origin of the enhanced electrochemical response.

item.title: JACS: Energy Deposition Timescale Controls Chemistry in Pulsed Methane Plasmas
item.description:
Norleakvisoth Lim, Michael J. Gordon
Nonoxidative methane conversion offers a promising route for the coproduction of hydrogen and value-added hydrocarbons without CO2 emissions. Among emerging approaches, pulsed plasmas can provide potential advantages by enabling high energy deposition, rapid quenching, and generation of active nonthermal species. This work systematically investigates how pulsed energy deposition from nanosecond-to-millisecond time scales (10 to 50 mJ/pulse) influences methane plasma characteristics (electron density and gas temperature), reaction mechanisms, conversion, and energy efficiency. Nanosecond discharges produced the highest overall C2 selectivity (>70%), with up to 20% for C2H4; in this regime, methane dissociation proceeded through both electron-impact and thermal dissociation, whereas longer pulses were predominantly thermal. Pulsed plasma conversion was similar to thermal arcs (∼377 kJ/mol CH4) and specific energy requirements to produce C2H2 and H2 were 15 kWh/kg and 40 kWh/kg, respectively, in 100 μs long discharges. The product distribution was largely determined by thermal processes involving dehydrogenation reactions (Kassel’s reaction scheme). High gas temperatures preferentially favored C2H2 formation over C2H4, and C2H4 selectivity decreased with increasing pulse width. Overall, these results demonstrate that pulse width and energy can be used to tailor hydrocarbon selectivity and can help design pulsed plasma systems for efficient production of value-added hydrocarbons and hydrogen.

item.title: JACS: Sky-Blue Thermally Activated Delayed Fluorescence from a Zirconium(IV) Complex
item.description:
Gage N. Jackson, Noura O. Ghader, Alexandra T. Barth, Brian S. Dolinar, Felix N. Castellano, Carsten Milsmann
Earth-abundant early transition-metal complexes with luminescent ligand-to-metal charge-transfer (LMCT) excited states remain an attractive yet underexplored alternative to widely used precious-metal emitters. A fundamental understanding of the molecular design principles governing the photophysical properties of LMCT emitters is critical to further developing cost-effective and sustainable photochemical applications using this compound class. Here, we report the synthesis of a novel bis(4,5-ditolylamido-9,9-dimethylxanthene)zirconium complex, Zr(TolXDA)2, that shows efficient photoluminescence due to thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) at room temperature. Steady-state and time-resolved spectroscopic studies at room temperature reveal highly efficient and long-lived emission in the sky-blue and green wavelength range for solid samples (λPL = 480 nm, ΦPL = 0.60, τPL = 4–14 μs) and THF solutions (λPL = 548 nm, ΦPL = 0.30, τPL = 8 μs) of Zr(TolXDA)2, respectively. Despite the relatively large singlet–triplet energy gap (ΔEST ≥ 0.26 eV), TADF emission in Zr(TolXDA)2 is unambiguously confirmed by temperature-dependent emission studies. This is likely facilitated by the high LMCT character of the S1 and T1 states, a consequence of strategic ligand design, which allows for rapid forward and reverse intersystem crossing. This hypothesis is supported by femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy, which confirms facile forward and reverse intersystem crossing in Zr(TolXDA)2 (τISC = 15 ± 5 ps, τrISC = 0.48 ± 0.39 μs), and TD-DFT calculations, which establish significant negative charge transfer to zirconium in the lowest energy excited states.

item.title: Nano Letters: Electron-Beam-Assisted Formation of Simple-Cubic Silver
item.description:
Masaya Sakakibara, Hiroki Nada, Yuji Kunisada, Tomoya Yamazaki, Yuki Kimura
Accessing crystal phases under nonequilibrium conditions is a central challenge for expanding the landscape of materials. Simple-cubic (sc) structures are considered energetically unfavorable in elemental solids and have previously been confirmed only in polonium. Here, we report the direct observation of a previously unrecognized sc-Ag formed under far-from-equilibrium conditions. Using electron beam irradiation inside a high-resolution transmission electron microscope as a trigger, we induced the radiolytic decomposition of silver iodide (AgI) and tracked the in situ formation of silver crystals in real time. Continuous imaging revealed that sc-Ag formation strongly depends on the polymorph of the precursor and occurs selectively from metastable γ-AgI. The sc-Ag exhibited unusually high chemical reactivity, undergoing gradual oxidation into silver oxide under high-vacuum conditions where conventional fcc-Ag remains stable. These findings demonstrate that irreversible crystal formation pathways can kinetically stabilize crystal structures inaccessible under near-equilibrium conditions and extend a previously inaccessible structural limit of metallic bonding.

item.title: ACS Nano: Zooming into the Cytoskeleton: Nanodefect-Initiated Microtubule Catastrophe Filmed by High-Speed Atomic Force Microscopy
item.description:
Xin Zhang, Keesiang Lim, Tomohiro Shima, Elma Sakinatus Sajidah, Masaharu Hazawa, Masahide Kikkawa, Toshio Ando, Richard W. Wong
Microtubule catastrophe is widely attributed to an end-driven loss of the GTP cap, implying that structural failure is confined to filament termini. Here, we show that this view is incomplete. Using high-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM), we directly visualize nanoscale structural failure in paclitaxel-treated microtubules in real time. We identify spontaneous lattice nanodefects that emerge within the filament shaft and act as internal initiation sites for disassembly. These defects arise from localized protofilament decoupling and lattice strain accumulation, which disrupt the cooperative interactions within the microtubule wall. Once a critical threshold is reached, these sites nucleate disassembly that propagates as distinct collapse trajectories, including bidirectional spreading from intralattice defects and inward convergence from opposing ends, in addition to classical end-initiated depolymerization. Rather than uniformly stabilizing the lattice, paclitaxel maintains microtubules in a metastable state in which internal stress heterogeneity persists and enables defect-driven failure. Our results establish lattice decoupling as a primary structural trigger of microtubule catastrophe and redefine it as a defect-mediated, spatially encoded transition. These findings provide a nanoscale mechanistic framework for understanding heterogeneous responses to microtubule-targeting chemotherapeutics, suggesting that drug resistance may arise from modulation of lattice integrity and defect propagation rather than drug binding alone.

item.title: Nano Letters: Cathodoluminescence Wavefront Retrieval
item.description:
Izzah Machfuudzoh, Ryoichi Horisaki, Takumi Sannomiya
Free-electron-based nanoscopy enables the study of optical excitations in materials with deep-subwavelength spatial resolution, with cathodoluminescence (CL) being one of the most useful signals. When combined with an optical collection system, CL measurements can access multidimensional information on light; yet the phase of the emitted optical fields has remained largely elusive. Here, we demonstrate a reference-free phase retrieval approach for far-field CL wavefronts using the Gerchberg–Saxton algorithm implemented with real-space and angular-space CL intensity data. Applying this approach to representative nanostructures, including a planar surface, nanosphere, plasmonic crystal, and nanowire, we reconstructed distinct phase distributions that revealed their underlying radiation mechanisms. This reference-free framework offers a robust and flexible route for retrieving the phase of electron beam-excited optical fields without relying on a reference wave, making it readily extendable to a wide range of nanostructures.

item.title: Nano Letters: Intra- and Interlayer Excitonic Fine Structure of the Two-Dimensional Perovskite (PEA)2PbI4
item.description:
Patrick Grenzer, Fabian Lie, Klaus H. Eckstein, Tobias Hertel, Linn Leppert
Two-dimensional halide perovskites host strongly bound excitons whose fine structure governs polarization selection rules and radiative recombination, yet spectral features in phenethylammonium lead iodide ((PEA)2PbI4) remain controversially assigned. Here, polarization-resolved low-temperature photoluminescence (PL) combined with first-principles G0W0+BSE calculations probes the intralayer and interlayer excitonic fine structure of this Ruddlesden–Popper perovskite. The low-energy multiplet is consistent with the intralayer excitonic fine structure governed by electron–hole exchange, crystal symmetry, and layer inequivalence in the two-layer unit cell, without requiring Rashba effects or exciton–polaron mechanisms as its primary origin. The weak doublet about 40 meV higher is best accounted for by interlayer excitons based on its energetics, splitting, and real-space character. Distortion-induced mixing of interlayer excitons with bright intralayer excitons provides a plausible explanation for the observed interlayer PL intensities and nearly orthogonal polarizations. These results support a layer-resolved excitonic picture encompassing both intralayer and interlayer states in (PEA)2PbI4.

item.title: Nano Letters: Magnetic Phase Diagram of Cr2Te3: The Hidden Role of Layer Stacking
item.description:
Cyriack Jego, Thierry Sauvage, Nicolas Gauthier, Quentin Guillet, Jean-François Jacquot, Isabelle Gomes de Moraes, Damien Caliste, Pascal Pochet, et al.
Using two-dimensional (2D) van der Waals (vdW) ferromagnets in spintronic devices can enhance their performance through well-controlled vdW interfaces and reduced power consumption. Cr2Te3 appears as a promising candidate because of its strong perpendicular magnetic anisotropy, but the Curie temperature is limited to 180 K. In this work, we use annealing in air to uncover the magnetic phase diagram of Cr2Te3. We correlate magnetic properties with layer stacking and the interlayer distance; both depend strongly on the annealing temperature. In particular, disorder in layer stacking plays a key role in the magnetic properties of Cr2Te3 and more generally of vdW ferromagnets. By annealing at 375 °C, we can eventually raise the Tc of Cr2Te3 up to 303 K in the epitaxial Cr2Te3/WSe2 vdW heterostructure with in-plane magnetic anisotropy. This work provides a simple method to control the magnetic properties of 2D ferromagnets and incorporate them into spintronics devices.

item.title: JACS: Physically Grounded Descriptors for Machine-Learning-Guided Diluent Design in Lithium Metal Batteries
item.description:
Myeongjun Kim, Chihyun Nam, Hyunmin Lee, Seyeon Shin, Songha Seo, Woojin Chong, Yejin Lee, Munsoo Song, et al.
Localized high-concentration electrolytes require diluents that avoid direct Li+ coordination and preserve Li+-anion aggregates while remaining miscible with the primary solvent. Rational discovery has remained difficult because these competing requirements arise from chemically distinct interactions that have lacked computable molecular design coordinates. Fluorination has therefore been widely used to suppress electron donation, but the environmental persistence and synthetic burden of fluorinated molecules motivate alternative strategies for controlling diluent functionality. Here, we resolve the key interaction requirements of diluents using two complementary descriptors: BF3 affinity for specific electron-pair donation and the molecular polarity index (MPI) for distributed nonspecific electrostatic interactions. These descriptors reproduce established donor-number and Kamlet–Taft π* trends and, more importantly, distinguish noncoordinating yet miscible diluents from solvating and immiscible solvents. Coupling this interaction-based framework with uncertainty-aware machine learning enabled screening of 1.32 million nonfluorinated molecules and identified 368 candidates while recovering false negatives and excluding false positives near the decision boundaries. Newly selected aromatic hydrocarbons, including 1,2,4-trimethylbenzene and 2-ethyltoluene, sustained stable cycling in Li-metal full cells for more than 200 cycles, whereas a descriptor-excluded analogue underwent rapid capacity decay. These results establish specific coordination and distributed electrostatics as predictive design coordinates for diluent discovery.

item.title: ACS Nano: Sliding Ferroelectric Tunnel Junctions with Ultrahigh Tunneling Electroresistance
item.description:
Haolin You, Chen Shao, Saagar Kolachina, Adrian Jonathan Lim, Robert Boyd, Chengdong Wang, Fan Fei, Carter Fox, et al.
Sliding ferroelectricity in van der Waals materials offers an appealing route to compact, nonvolatile, atomically thin ferroelectric tunnel junctions (FTJs) with low switching energy, but achieving a large resistance contrast in such devices remains challenging because the weak out-of-plane polarization provides limited electrostatic modulation of the tunneling barrier. Here, using bilayer rhombohedral MoS2 as a sliding ferroelectric barrier, we demonstrate room-temperature sliding FTJs with tunneling electroresistance (TER) values exceeding 3.2 × 105. We show that this giant contrast arises from a height–width hybrid tunneling mechanism, in which polarization reversal simultaneously modulates the tunnel barrier height and switches a nanoscale interfacial depletion width, yielding exponential amplification of the tunneling contrast. Spatially resolved tunneling, piezoresponse, and Raman measurements reveal that local strain, rather than ferroelectric domain walls, dominates spatial variations in the TER by modulating the sliding ferroelectric dipole strength, the OFF-state depletion width, and the resulting TER amplification. Finally, planar 3R-MoS2 FTJs further validate this mechanism by exhibiting a TER above 105, a switching energy density of several fJ μm–2, and projected endurance beyond 106. These results provide fundamental insight into the nanoscale electrostatics in sliding ferroelectric-based tunnel junctions while pointing toward low-energy, high-contrast nonvolatile memory applications.

item.title: ACS Nano: Peptide Coacervates with Cathepsin B-Triggered Intracellular Cargo Release
item.description:
Pooja Sharma, Soheil Haddadzadegan, Mahsa Ghafouri, Sushanth Gudlur, Ali Miserez
Understanding the molecular grammar of liquid–liquid phase separation has enabled rational design of peptide coacervates as intracellular therapeutic carriers with tunable viscoelasticity, controlled cargo partitioning, and enhanced cellular uptake. However, sequence-level determinants governing coacervate disassembly remain poorly characterized. Encoding protease-recognition motifs within phase-separating peptides offers controlled, localized catalytic disassembly without requiring global perturbation via macroscopic triggers such as pH, ionic strength, temperature, or redox potential. Yet, enzymatic cleavage of coacervates is spatially biased and constrained by limited enzyme partitioning, restricted substrate accessibility, and altered kinetics relative to the dilute phase. Here, we test whether the lysosomal protease cathepsin B (CatB)─often upregulated in cancer cells─acts on coacervates assembled from phase-separating peptides encoding CatB-recognition motifs to enable intracellular cargo release in cancer cells. Common CatB-recognition motifs (GFLG and EVCit), developed for linker-based delivery systems under dilute conditions, preserved phase separation but exhibited poor CatB-triggered cleavage and cargo release. In contrast, a de novo motif, FRFV, designed from CatB subsite preferences, retained catalytic activity as confirmed by mass spectrometry and enabled protease-triggered cargo release in vitro and in cancer cells. Thus, protease-recognition motifs require reevaluation within dense-phase architectures to enable efficient intracellular cargo release through coacervate disassembly.

item.title: JACS: Thiol-Mediated Hydrazide Installation from Diazo in the Biosynthesis of Spinamycin
item.description:
Haoran Pang, Wenni Zhang, Wenjun Zhang
Natural products featuring nitrogen–nitrogen (N–N) bonds often possess potent bioactivities, and their architectures frequently reveal novel enzymatic mechanisms. Current understanding for acylhydrazide installation is limited to a “hydrazine-first” strategy, wherein an activated acyl donor is nucleophilically attacked by a preassembled hydrazine intermediate. Spinamycin, an antifungal hydrazide-containing aryl polyene from Streptomyces albospinus, challenges this convention. Its biosynthetic machinery utilizes SpiA7, an ATP-dependent, nitrite-utilizing N-nitrosylase, to synthesize a highly transient diazo intermediate rather than a hydrazine core. How this unstable diazo compound is converted into a stable hydrazide has remained a long-standing biosynthetic mystery. Herein, we report the in vitro reconstitution of the activity of SpiA7 in conversion of the amine substrate into its mature succinylhydrazide form. Mechanistic characterization revealed that the electrophilic diazo intermediate is initially captured by thiol reagents to generate a covalent azo-sulfide intermediate (R–N═N–S–R′). This species likely undergoes a noncanonical four-electron reduction driven cooperatively by disulfide bond formation and the oxidative decarboxylation of α-ketoglutarate (αKG), which serves as the succinyl donor. Furthermore, site-directed mutagenesis identifies Cys453 of SpiA7 as a likely active-site thiol donor orchestrating this transformation. Collectively, our findings unveil an unprecedented chemical strategy for hydrazide assembly that completely bypasses a free hydrazine intermediate, expanding nature’s known catalytic repertoire for building complex N–N linkages.

item.title: JACS: Bridging Ionic Field Strength Disparity in O3-Type Layered Oxides for High-Voltage Sodium-Ion Batteries
item.description:
Ziheng Zhang, Zixin Liang, Yixiang Zhao, Jiangtao Yu, Mengchen Zhang, Ji Kong, Yanxia Deng, Zhiwei Yu, et al.
O3-type layered oxides represent an attractive class of sodium-ion battery cathodes, combining high theoretical specific capacity and high pristine Na content. However, their deeply desodiated frameworks at high voltages (≥4.0 V) are prone to redox-coupled distortion of TMO6 octahedra within the transition metal (TM) slabs, leading to severe structural degradation. Here, we originally define an ionic field strength disparity coefficient (η), which enables quantitative evaluation of the local chemical-field heterogeneity. The η is derived from the ratio between the standard deviation and the average value of ionic field strength (Φ) of all TM ions, defined as Φ= Z/r2, where Z and r correspond to the ionic charge and ionic radius, respectively. Introducing compensatory cations with an intermediate Φ value between two cations featuring largely disparate Φ values effectively reconciles local chemical-field discrepancy and lowers the η parameter upon charge–discharge processes. Moreover, synchrotron X-ray absorption spectroscopy, strain mapping analyses, and first-principles calculations reveal that the low-η sample demonstrates the reduced lattice strain and enhanced structural reversibility. Consistently, electrochemical evaluation shows that it retains more than 80% of its capacity after 500 cycles at 10C, markedly outperforming the unmodified counterpart with only 22% retention. This work establishes the η as a quantitative descriptor for inactive dopant selection and provides a general strategy for developing highly stable layered oxide cathodes.

item.title: JACS: Microenvironment-Directed Galvanostatic Base Generation for Near-Neutral Hydrolysis of a Nerve-Agent Simulant
item.description:
Sohui Kim, Mansu Kim, Hyung-Suk Oh, Dongmok Whang, Joseph T. Hupp
Organophosphate hydrolysis under near-neutral conditions is intrinsically slow and generally requires strongly basic media or tailored catalysts. Here, we demonstrate that the electrolyte microenvironment can promote hydrolysis of dimethyl 4-nitrophenyl phosphate (DMNP) through an electrochemically generated base. Chemical controls show that DMNP hydrolysis depends on the combined effects of bulk pH, phosphate speciation, electrolyte concentration, and substrate accessibility. Under galvanostatic operation, cathodic water reduction generates OH– in situ, coupling hydrogen evolution to specific-base SN2(P) hydrolysis of DMNP. Time-resolved 31P NMR shows reciprocal DMNP consumption and dimethyl phosphate formation, while complementary UV–vis spectroscopy is consistent with formation of p-nitrophenolate. Although K2HPO4 and NaClO4 provide similar DMNP conversion at the same current, phosphate lowers the required overpotential and substantially improves energy-normalized conversion efficiency. Translation to a zero-gap membrane-electrode assembly enables stable full-cell operation and quantitative DMNP consumption within 1 h in a larger-volume, flow-compatible configuration. These findings establish galvanostatic in situ base generation as a controllable and modular strategy for organophosphate treatment in near-neutral aqueous media.

item.title: JACS: Molecule-Driven Unusual Incommensurate Modulation in a 2D Hybrid Perovskite Ferroelectric
item.description:
Lijun Xu, Hongfei Ma, Ji Qi, Hang Li, Chengshu Zhang, Huang Ye, Haiqing Zhong, Yuan Yu, et al.
Incommensurate modulation has been extensively investigated in inorganic oxides, representing an emerging frontier in aperiodic materials that enables the discovery of novel quantum phenomena and the manipulation of physical properties, whereas it remains largely unexplored in hybrid perovskites (HPs). Here, we present the driving of successive dynamic rotation of the interlayer dipoles in a two-dimensional HP ferroelectric (DFBZ)2(FA)Pb2I7 (DFBZ is 2,5-difluorobenzylammonium, FA is formamidinium), which enables an unusual incommensurate modulated structure between the paraelectric and ferroelectric phases. Specifically, (DFBZ)2(FA)Pb2I7 exhibits an incommensurate modulated state over a broad temperature range of 313–370 K, and transforms to commensurate modulation at 400–474 K. The incommensurate superstructure at 330 K is ∼6 times larger than its periodic prototype, and its structure can be solved using a (3 + 1)D superspace group with a modulation wavevector of q = (1, 0, 0.1578). The inorganic layers feature a pronounced undulation, while the interlayer organic cations are trapped in distinct rotational states. To the best of our knowledge, (DFBZ)2(FA)Pb2I7 is the first HP ferroelectric that exhibits such a long-range ordered incommensurate modulation. Moreover, its large spontaneous polarization (9.4 μC cm–2) and the near-room temperature ferroelectric-to-incommensurate phase transition result in a giant pyroelectric coefficient of 7.41 μC cm–2 K–1. This unusual incommensurate modulation in HP ferroelectrics offers new insights into the understanding of aperiodic materials and ferroelectric mechanisms.

item.title: JACS: Deoxygenative Metal Carbenation: A Strategy for Stereocontrolled Olefin Metathesis via an Oxo-Ruthenium Precursor
item.description:
Samantha K. Cormier, Harrison C. Max, Eliza-Jayne Y. Boisvert, Michael J. Ferguson, Deryn E. Fogg
Dithiolene metathesis catalysts have enabled breakthroughs in materials and medicinal contexts in which control of cis/trans alkene stereochemistry translates into control over function. Their extreme air-sensitivity, however, impedes widespread uptake. Building on the discovery that air-exposure selectively decomposes the leading catalyst Ru(S–S)(H2IPr)(═CHAr) (Ru-1a; S–S = 1,2-S2C6H2-3,6-Cl2, Ar = C6H4-2-OiPr) into four-coordinate oxo complex Ru-2 Ru(O)(S–S)(H2IPr), we demonstrate that the latter offers convenient access to Ru-1a and related catalysts via reaction with phosphorus ylides (Ph3P═CHR; R = Ar, Ph, H). This “deoxygenative metal carbenation” (DMC) strategy opens new opportunities in olefin metathesis. Beyond regeneration of Ru-1a after decomposition, it enables direct, tunable access to more active on-cycle species (potentially including tagged benzylidenes) from a robust, shelf-stable precursor. In situ generation of these well-defined active species confers metathesis activity and stereocontrol comparable to or better than pristine, meticulously handled Ru-1a, and far superior to samples of Ru-1a even briefly exposed to air in solution. In eliminating the need for production, shipping, and storage of air-sensitive Ru-1a, this advance is anticipated to expand the uptake of olefin metathesis for production of stereodefined alkenes.

item.title: JACS: A Route to Enhanced Energy Barriers and Reduced Magnetic Relaxation in Axial Bis(stannolediide) Lanthanidocenates
item.description:
Xiaofei Sun, Concepción Molina-Jirón, Masaichi Saito, Sagar Paul, Mario Ruben, Wolfgang Wernsdorfer, Eufemio Moreno-Pineda, Peter W. Roesky
We report the synthesis and magnetic properties of one-dimensional lanthanidocenate coordination polymers, [Ln(η5-LSn)2K]n (Ln = Tb, Dy; LSn = [1,4-bis(tert-butyl-dimethylsilyl)-2,3-bis-phenyl-stannolediide]). These were obtained by abstracting the solvent molecules from the potassium atoms of the corresponding monomers [Ln(η5-LSn)2K(thf)4]. The flexible coordination of the stannole dianion enables polymerization via potassium-mediated Sn–K–arene interactions, yielding linear chain structures while preserving a highly axial coordination environment around the Ln3+ center. Magnetic studies reveal that both [Ln(η5-LSn)2K]n (Ln = Tb, Dy) compounds behave as single-molecule magnets in zero field, with significantly enhanced performance compared to their monomeric analogues. In particular, [Dy(η5-LSn)2K]n exhibits an increased effective energy barrier of Ueff = 1812 K, representing an improvement of ∼20%, alongside suppressed quantum tunneling of magnetization and slower relaxation dynamics. Detailed analysis of the relaxation mechanisms indicates that polymerization reduces spin–phonon coupling, as evidenced by a marked suppression of the Raman relaxation process, despite softer lattice vibrational modes. Ab initio calculations confirm the retention of highly axial electronic structures. These results demonstrate that assembling axial lanthanidocenate units into one-dimensional frameworks is an effective strategy to enhance magnetic anisotropy and control relaxation pathways, providing a route to mitigate relaxation in high-performance lanthanide-based single-molecule magnets.

item.title: JACS: Directional Charge Transport via Interlayer Electronic Coupling Enhances Photocatalysis in Covalent Organic Frameworks
item.description:
Zhongliang Wen, Titus de Haas, Jiamin Sun, Diem Van Hamme, Chidharth Krishnaraj, Annelies Vitharana, Maojun Deng, Linyang Wang, et al.
The design of efficient photocatalysts requires control over both exciton dissociation and the subsequent transport of charge carriers. Donor–acceptor two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are widely used to promote charge separation, but the role of directional charge transport in these layered materials is still not well understood. Here, we combine photophysical characterization and time-dependent density functional theory calculations to study three TAPD-based COFs for photocatalytic H2O2 production via oxygen reduction. All materials show efficient in-plane donor–acceptor charge transfer with similar exciton dissociation behavior. At the same time, clear differences appear in their charge transport properties. The calculations indicate that electrons move preferentially along the stacking direction, while holes remain more delocalized within the COF plane. This anisotropic transport is most pronounced in the COFs where stronger interlayer coupling favors the formation of interlayer charge-transfer states, as observed in transient absorption measurements. These states allow electrons and holes to separate over adjacent layers, which reduces recombination losses and corroborates the observed differences in photocatalytic activity. Our results indicate that directional interlayer charge transport, rather than local donor–acceptor charge separation alone, is an important factor in determining photocatalytic performance in COFs.

item.title: JACS: Physics-Informed Site-Specific Molecular Interaction Learning Framework for Liquid–Liquid Phase Diagram Reconstruction and Extraction Process Design
item.description:
Jinlin Ye, Shuohan Wang, Hongchang Zhang, Yankang Liu, Junhao Wang, Ziyang Zhang, Xin Yang, Kai Li, et al.
Liquid–liquid phase behavior is governed by the collective balance of intermolecular interactions and is central to predicting component partitioning and designing extraction-based separation processes. Existing thermodynamic and data-driven approaches can predict phase-equilibrium properties, but provide limited resolution of the molecular-interaction-to-phase-topology relationship underlying coupled binodal boundaries and tie-line families. Here, PSMI is proposed as a physics-informed site-specific molecular interaction learning framework that reconstructs ternary liquid–liquid phase diagrams directly from molecular structures. PSMI learns chemically meaningful intermolecular interaction sites through molecular representation learning and integrates chemical-potential consistency regularization to guide thermodynamically reliable phase reconstruction. The framework predicts coexisting extract and raffinate compositions along continuous phase paths and enables reconstruction of binodal boundaries and tie-line families. Across benchmark tests, PSMI accurately predicts coexisting extract and raffinate compositions and recovers phase-diagram topology, including both binodal shapes and tie-line directions. Interpretability analysis shows that PSMI identifies transferable molecular drivers underlying liquid–liquid phase separation, including chemically meaningful interaction patterns. Industrial case studies, together with a locally deployable web application, further demonstrate the practical utility and accessibility of PSMI for solvent screening and extraction process design. By resolving site-specific intermolecular interactions together with their macroscopic phase-partitioning consequences, PSMI provides a molecular-level perspective on how local chemical environments contribute to liquid–liquid phase behavior. This connection between localized molecular interactions and continuous phase-diagram topology provides a framework for understanding and designing complex liquid–liquid separation systems.

item.title: ACS Nano: Stress-Resilient Skin Wound Protection via Bioinspired Dual-Tier Architecture
item.description:
Xinxin Zhao, Zhao Pan, Jingjing Zhang, Mohan Wang, Pan Zhang, Rui Xu, Huailing Gao, Xinyue Wang, et al.
Mechanical tension destabilizes wound repair and drives fibrotic progression, yet current protection materials rarely reconcile the contrasting requirements of load-bearing and interfacial adaptability. To address this persistent mechanical conflict, a dual-tier hydrogel architecture was developed by integrating a stiff protective tier with a compliant adaptive tier to redistribute deformation and maintain secure adhesion under load. The stiff tier intercepted external stress, the compliant tier accommodated deformation, and dual interfaces regulated force transmission to avoid stress concentration on wound sites. The construct preserved bioadhesion energy exceeded that of various commercial products, and ex vivo distraction tests showed controlled wound opening with deformation control ratios of 70–90% compared with 30–40% for the commercial Mepiform patch. In a tension-driven murine model, the dual-tier patch demonstrated a reduction in scar area of approximately 97%, restored collagen angular dispersion and fiber diameter toward unwounded patterns, and lowered proliferative, inflammatory, immune, and mechanotransduction signals with significant improvement over Mepiform. These findings underscore the value of architecture-driven material design for achieving stable wound protection under fluctuating mechanical conditions.

item.title: JACS: Secondary-Sphere Control of Electronic Structure and Ligand Basicity in Mo-Nitrogenase: A QM/MM Analysis Guided by Se K-Edge HERFD XAS
item.description:
Gursahib Singh Sethi, Justin P. Joyce, Christina Roemelt, Kushal Sengupta, Serena DeBeer
Molybdenum nitrogenase catalyzes biological nitrogen fixation using a complex metallocofactor (FeMoco) containing three μ2-“belt”sulfides that exhibit distinct reactivity during catalysis. In particular, protonation at the S2B site imparts lability that facilitates substrate binding and may enable this sulfide to act as a proton donor. Although FeMoco is inactive outside its protein environment, how secondary-sphere residues tune its geometric and electronic structure to enable function remains unclear. We have previously shown that site-selective Se substitution of the μ2-sulfides provides a direct probe of the ligand environment using Se K-edge high-energy-resolution fluorescence-detected X-ray absorption spectroscopy (HERFD XAS). Despite the cofactor’s approximate C3 symmetry, Se-substituted sites display pronounced differences in Se HERFD XAS pre-edge intensities. Utilizing QM/MM calculations, we show that hydrogen-bonding (H-bonding) residues polarize the S3A and S5A sulfides, reducing metal–ligand covalency and attenuating pre-edge intensity, whereas hydrophobic residues surrounding S2B localize electron density and enhance its pre-edge intensity. These results demonstrate how hydrophobicity and H-bonding within the secondary coordination sphere modulate FeMoco electronic structure. More broadly, they show how the protein environment tunes ligand basicity to favor selective S2B protonation and provide design principles for controlling enzymatic function.

item.title: JACS: Cryo-EM Structure of a Monomeric Safracin B Nonribosomal Peptide Synthetase Enabled by an MbtH-like Protein and Covalent Probe Trapping
item.description:
Naoto Haraguchi, Kanami Takahashi, Kana Matsuda, Kiichi Honda, Ryo Tanifuji, Takashi Matsui, Takeshi Yokoyama, Christos Gatsogiannis, et al.
Nonribosomal peptide synthetases (NRPSs) assemble structurally complex natural products but remain challenging targets for high-resolution structural analysis because of their conformational heterogeneity and dynamic catalytic cycles. SacC/SfmC is an unusual single-module NRPS that diverges from canonical peptide-forming assembly lines and instead catalyzes two sequential Pictet–Spengler reactions between a tyrosine-derived unit and a peptidyl aldehyde generated through thioester reduction. This cascade forms two C–C bonds, stereoselectively installs multiple stereogenic centers, and constructs the pentacyclic scaffold of bis-tetrahydroisoquinoline antitumor alkaloids including safracin B and the clinically important ecteinascidins. Here, we establish a state-resolved cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) strategy for structural interrogation of the monomeric noncanonical NRPS SacC and report its thioesterification-state structure at 2.76 Å resolution. Stabilization of this transient catalytic state was achieved by combining the cognate MbtH-like partner protein with a tailored covalent adenosine vinylsulfonamide probe that mimics the aminoacyl-adenylate intermediate and traps the phosphopantetheine-tethered species within the adenylation domain. The structure directly visualizes a carrier protein-tethered intermediate and reveals the spatial organization of the Pictet–Spengler, adenylation, peptidyl carrier protein, and reduction domains, providing the first structural view of a Pictet–Spengler cyclization domain embedded within an NRPS assembly line. In parallel, nonreducible ester probes corresponding to downstream PCP-bound intermediates were developed to enable structural interrogation of additional catalytic states along the SacC reaction trajectory. These results demonstrate that rational chemical probe design enables state-resolved cryo-EM analysis of highly dynamic, single-module NRPSs and establishes a general strategy for capturing catalytic trajectories and enabling the engineering of noncanonical NRPS reactivity.

item.title: JACS: Selective Methylation of Phenol with CO2/H2 to o -Cresol and 2,6-Xylenol
item.description:
Changxin He, Jiaxin Zhang, Junqi Tian, Jun Yuan, Hongfang Yang, Ruihui Zhang, Zhihe Mao, Xiaojing Wu, et al.
Employing CO2/H2 as a sustainable methylating agent offers a transformative strategy for advancing conventional methylation processes, yet achieving controllable C–C coupling with high efficiency remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report a novel tandem process that integrates CO2 hydrogenation with phenol methylation over a Zr-doped In2O3 solid-solution catalyst. The optimized In7Zr3Ox catalyst exhibits >95% selectivity toward ortho-methylation with tunable product distribution, ranging from 92% o-cresol at 16% conversion to 86% 2,6-xylenol at 97% conversion, while maintaining stable operation for 140 h. Mechanistic studies identify surface formaldehyde species (CH2O*) generated from CO2 hydrogenation as the active methylating intermediates that kinetically couple CO2 reduction to phenol methylation. This pathway exhibits a markedly lower apparent activation energy of 58.8 kJ mol–1 than the conventional methanol-mediated route of 116.3 kJ mol–1. Continuous consumption of CH2O* also shifts the CO2 hydrogenation equilibrium, imparting a thermodynamic driving effect absent in CO2 hydrogenation alone. These findings demonstrate the potential of CO2-based methylation for selective C–C bond formation and expand opportunities for CO2 valorization.

item.title: Nano Letters: Curvature-Controlled Polar–Dislocation Coupling in Freestanding Ferroelectric Oxide Heterostructures
item.description:
Jianwei Liang, Yi Huang, Gangchang Li, Congbing Tan, Wenpeng Zhu, Yi Zhang, Yue Zheng
Curvature couples polarization, crystalline defects, and interfacial electrostatics in freestanding ferroelectric oxides. Here, we examine bent epitaxial Pb(Zr0.2Ti0.8)O3/SrTiO3/Pb(Zr0.2Ti0.8)O3 (PZT/STO/PZT) membranes using atomic-resolution electron microscopy, strain and polarization mapping, relative projected-potential reconstruction, and molecular dynamics simulations. The tensile-side PZT remains comparatively lattice-continuous and accommodates bending mainly through polarization rotation and domain reorganization. The compressive-side PZT exhibits dislocations, slip-related lattice offsets, surface steps, and localized strain concentration. Curvature-series observations and images across U-shaped and N-shaped regions indicate that the defect-rich region follows the local compressive stress state. Bending also breaks the approximate electrostatic symmetry of the two PZT/STO interfaces: the tensile side shows weakened negative interfacial contrast, whereas the compressive side shows a dislocation-associated increase in relative projected potential. These results identify curvature as a variable for selecting polar versus plastic relaxation pathways and modulating interfacial electrostatic landscapes in flexible ferroelectric heterostructures.

item.title: JACS: A New Paradigm for Computational Chemistry
item.description:
Raphael T. Husistein, Markus Reiher
Computational chemistry has become an indispensable tool for generating data and insights, pervading all branches of experimental chemistry. Its most central concept is the potential energy hypersurface, which is key to all chemistry and materials science, as it assigns an energy to a molecular structure, the necessary ingredient for reaction mechanism elucidation and reaction rate calculation. Density functional theory (DFT) has been the most important method in practice for obtaining such energies, which is reflected in the use of high-performance computing hardware. In the last two decades, a new class of surrogate potential energy functions has evolved with remarkable properties: quantum accuracy combined with force-field speed. Until very recently, their application was hampered by the fact that they needed to be trained on truly large system-specific data sets, generated before a computational chemistry study could be started (in sharp contrast to DFT, which, as a first-principles method, works out of the box but at a far higher price of computational cost). Very recently, this roadblock has been overcome by so-called foundation machine learning interatomic potentials, which are poised to completely change the way we do computational chemistry, likely prompting us to abandon DFT as the prime method of choice for this purpose in less than a decade.

item.title: ACS Nano: Low Energy Excitations in a [4]Triangulene Honeycomb Antiferromagnet
item.description:
Aidan Delgado, Carolin Dusold, James Wu, Jingwei Jiang, Christina M. Dadich, Adam Cronin, Steven G. Louie, Felix R. Fischer
Carbon-based synthetic lattices offer a versatile platform for the realization and control of correlated quantum effects at the nanoscale. Advances in on-surface synthesis have enabled the fabrication of increasingly complex molecular frameworks, providing opportunities for the exploration and engineering of custom tailored electronic and magnetic phases. Here, we report the design, on-surface synthesis, and characterization of a two-dimensional (2D) covalent organic framework (COF) assembled from D3h symmetric S = 3/2 [4]triangulene building blocks arranged in a honeycomb structure. Combined scanning probe microscopy and spectroscopy, corroborated by first-principles density functional theory (DFT) and GW calculations, establish an antiferromagnetic (AFM) insulating ground state. Low energy spectroscopy resolves spin excitations in both one-dimensional (1D) chains and extended 2D networks, providing direct insight into the emergent spin dynamics and establishing a modular platform to explore quantum magnetism in a π-conjugated organic system.

item.title: JACS: Radical SAM Enzymes Catalyze Aromatic–Proline Cross-Links in Lanthipeptide Biosynthesis
item.description:
Ye Lei Zhou, Jing Shi, Jing Xin Zhang, Zi Fei Xu, Yi Ling Hu, Fang Zhou Yin, Zhang Yuan Yan, Zhi Kai Guo, et al.
Radical S-adenosylmethionine (rSAM) enzymes enable some of the most chemically challenging transformations in natural product biosynthesis, profoundly shaping the structural diversity of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs). Despite extensive studies in several RiPP families, the contribution of rSAM chemistry to lanthipeptide biosynthesis has remained poorly defined. Here, we identify a widespread group of rSAM enzymes associated with type III/IV lanthipeptide gene clusters through combined genome mining and phylogenetic analysis. Characterization of representative pathways uncovered a series of new lanthipeptides bearing an N-terminal aromatic–proline carbon–carbon cross-link. Detailed LC–MS/MS and NMR analyses revealed that Trp, Phe, or His residues are covalently linked to a conserved Pro residue, establishing a broader family of rSAM-catalyzed aromatic–proline couplings in lanthipeptide biosynthesis. Notably, biochemical reconstitution, active-site mutagenesis, substrate profiling, and isotope-labeling experiments define key catalytic requirements, support a radical-mediated dehydrogenative coupling mechanism, and show that lanthionine formation is not an absolute prerequisite for AitR-catalyzed aromatic–proline cross-linking. These findings broaden the substrate and structural scope of rSAM-catalyzed cross-linking in lanthipeptide RiPPs.

item.title: Nano Letters: Flexible Microlaser Emitter for Mechanical Sensing and Pulse Mapping
item.description:
Ningyuan Nie, Zhiyi Yuan, Tian Zhou, Guocheng Fang, Bowen Fu, Xiyu Sun, Po-Hao Tseng, Yu-Cheng Chen
Flexible photonic devices and soft microlasers have attracted increasing attention for wearable sensing, biomedical monitoring, and deformable optoelectronic systems. Their mechanical compliance enables intimate contact with soft biological tissues, allowing optical signals to be modulated by external mechanical stimuli. Such characteristics make flexible laser-based platforms particularly suitable for mechanical sensing and physiological signal detection. In this work, we present a flexible microlaser array-based photonic platform designed for mechanical sensing and pulse monitoring. By integrating microscale laser emitters into a soft, transparent matrix with a microstructured architecture, the device maintains stable laser emission while responding to external pressure and dynamic strain. The optical response of the microlaser array exhibits sensitivity to mechanical perturbations, enabling the detection of periodic signals associated with the human pulse. This work highlights the potential of flexible laser photonics as a versatile tool for noninvasive mechanical and physiological sensing in wearable healthcare applications.

item.title: ACS Nano: Crown Ether-Functionalized Covalent Organic Framework Membranes for Precise Monovalent Cation Separation
item.description:
Ziye Song, Kai Liu, Wendi Zhang, William Wang Dirckinck-Holmfeld, Saisai Yu, Zhe Jia, Yuanhan Liu, Yutao Guan, et al.
